title: Iterator pattern
idea: The Iterator pattern gives callers a cursor that visits a collection's elements one by one, without revealing how the collection stores them.
points: The collection implements `Iterable` and hands out a fresh `Iterator` per traversal.
Each iterator keeps its own position, so two loops never disturb each other.
Java's for-each loop calls `iterator()`, then `hasNext()` and `next()` for you.
Skip a custom iterator when a list will do; return `List.copyOf` or a stream.

hero.title: One for-each loop, message by message

messages.label: iterator()
messages.note: The loop asks the collection for a cursor. It never sees the array inside.

messages.label: new Cursor()
messages.note: The cursor starts at index 0 and records the list's current `modCount`.

messages.label: hasNext()
messages.note: The loop asks first. The cursor compares its index with `size`, not the array length.

messages.label: next() -> Intro
messages.note: `next()` returns one element and moves the cursor forward by one.

messages.label: add("Bonus")
messages.note: Someone changes the playlist mid-loop. Its `modCount` moves past the cursor's snapshot.

messages.label: next()
messages.note: The cursor sees the version changed and refuses to guess.

messages.label: ConcurrentModification
messages.note: Fail-fast: an exception now beats silently skipping or repeating an element later.

code.title: The problem: leaked storage
code.caption: The playlist hands out its raw array. Callers must know its layout, and they can change it.

walk.text: Storage is an array with spare slots plus a count. That is an internal detail.
Returning the array itself leaks that detail to every caller.
The loop trusts `raw.length`, so it plays an empty slot: see the `null` line.
Another caller overwrites a song. The playlist cannot stop it or even notice.
Switch to a linked list later and both clients fail to compile.

code.title: The fix: Iterable + cursor
code.caption: The playlist hides its array behind `Iterable`. Its iterator is independent, bounded and fail-fast.

walk.text: Implementing `Iterable` is the whole public contract. For-each now works on `Playlist`.
A private inner class reads the array directly; nobody outside can reach it.
Two cursors, two positions: advancing `a` does not move `b`.
Bounds come from `size`, so spare array slots are never returned.
Past the end, `next()` throws `NoSuchElementException`, as the `Iterator` contract requires.
A version counter detects changes during a loop and fails fast, like `ArrayList` does.
Adding inside the loop trips the check on the next call to `next()`.

pitfalls: A getter returning the internal array lets callers corrupt state; return an iterator or copy.
Calling `list.remove` in a for-each loop may throw or silently skip; use `Iterator.remove` or `removeIf`.
Storing the cursor in the collection, not the iterator, makes nested loops over one list interfere.

quiz.why: Removing `b` makes size 2 while the cursor is at 2. `hasNext()` returns false, so the loop silently skips `c` and nothing throws.

takeaway: Expose a cursor, not your storage; each loop gets its own.

starters: How would I write an iterator that filters or skips elements lazily?
Why is ArrayList's iterator fail-fast but CopyOnWriteArrayList's is not?
When is returning a Stream better than implementing Iterable?
